query: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy previously showed limited amorphous retention and a complicated thermal response. Earlier thermal studies of Ni–P and Pd–Ni–P alloys found that rapid quenching could produce amorphous material, but that its stability was limited during subsequent heating. The design challenge is therefore to obtain robust glass formation across relevant cooling conditions without sacrificing stability during reheating. What single intervention could improve amorphous retention and thermal stability during solidification and thermal analysis? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the reported behavior of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, the cooling-rate and reheating conditions under which it should or should not succeed, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a rare‐earth element (e.g. ~1 at% Gd) to the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy will improve glass‐forming ability and increase thermal stability during both rapid solidification and subsequent reheating.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 which shows limited amorphous retention and complex crystallization upon reheating.
generation.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of ≈1 at% Gd into the base Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 composition.
generation.conditions: This intervention is expected to be effective under high cooling rate conditions (e.g., melt-spinning producing cooling rates on the order of 10^5–10^6 K/s) where amorphous structuring is normally obtained, and during subsequent moderate reheating (as investigated via DSC) that typically triggers crystallization in the unmodified alloy. It may be less effective under very slow cooling regimes where crystallization is dominant.
generation.structural_mediator: The introduction of Gd increases atomic size mismatch and disrupts local atomic ordering, thereby raising the liquid viscosity and retarding the kinetics of nucleation during solidification. This effectively stabilizes the metastable amorphous structure and shifts crystallization to higher temperatures upon reheating.
generation.mechanism: Gd microalloying enhances the configurational entropy and creates local structural frustration. This delays the onset of crystallization both during rapid cooling and upon modest reheating, compared to the unmodified Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy. The mechanism is analogous to prior observations in Ni–P and Pd–Ni–P systems, where microalloying with elements of significantly different atomic radii (such as Gd) improved the glass-forming ability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the base alloy, the Gd‐modified alloy will exhibit a more robust amorphous phase over a broader range of cooling rates and show a higher crystallization onset temperature (or reduced exothermic crystallization peak) during heating. This indicates improved thermal stability of the amorphous phase without sacrificing formation during rapid quenching.
generation.baseline: The reported behavior of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, which under very fast cooling forms an amorphous structure that transforms on reheating with complex, multi‐phase crystallization.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected at low microalloying levels (around 1 at%); higher concentrations might destabilize the overall composition or induce other phases. In addition, under very slow cooling conditions (e.g., <100 K/s), crystallization may occur regardless of the Gd addition, limiting the intervention's effectiveness.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative benefits of microalloying with Gd are supported by analogous studies in Ni–P systems, the quantitative shifts in crystallization temperatures and the optimal concentration in Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni–P systems remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys by arc melting: one set of the base Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy and one set with ~1 at% Gd added (with a compensating reduction in one of the other elements to maintain overall composition). Process both sets under identical rapid cooling conditions (e.g., via melt-spinning at 10^5–10^6 K/s) and subject samples to controlled reheating using DSC. Characterize their phases by XRD and TEM before and after reheating.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine onset temperatures and enthalpies of crystallization.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess the amorphous vs. crystalline phase content.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural confirmation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Gd-alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., >50 K) increase in the crystallization onset temperature or reduced crystallization exotherm compared to the base alloy, and if the fraction of retained amorphous phase is similar or lower than that of the base alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Its inclusion in Ni-Fe-Cu-P-Si-B alloys also enables the development of extremely soft magnetic materials, broadening the potential applications of these alloys []. Furthermore, recent findings on NiNbP bulk metallic glasses highlight how phosphorus additions enhance glass-forming ability and increase hardness, albeit at the cost of some ductility []. Inspired by these results, this study explores the microstructure, mechanical behavior, and phase stability of phosphorus-containing alloys to better understand and utilize their unique properties. The combination of high configurational entropy and phosphorus enrichment in these alloys suggests their potential for applications in demanding environments that require enhanced wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability. These properties position them as promising candidates for use in the aerospace, automotive, and tooling industries, as well as in advanced coating technologies and high-performance structural components. To investigate the impact of small concentrations of an additionally added element on a glass-forming alloy, the critical cooling rates and glass formation regions are computed for the Pd-Ni-P-system micro-alloyed with 1 at% of Co, Cu, Fe, and Gd. Micro-alloying of Co, Cu, and Fe had little effect on the overall glass-forming ability which matches well with experimental results for (Pd40Ni40P20)99Co1 and (Pd40Ni40P20)99.4Fe0.6 that showed an impact on the mechanical properties without affecting the glass formation properties in a significant way (see Figure 6) [,]. This behavior is to be expected within the framework of the current model since cobalt, copper, and iron are similar in atomic weight and radius to nickel and therefore will not impact the calculation. This is different for gadolinium, since it varies in its properties significantly from the former alloying elements. The impact of the micro-alloying of gadolinium is even noticeable for concentrations below 1 at% as shown in Figure 6 within the employed model.
